pool.prompt: What does NESC Section 35 govern, and to which cable types does it apply?
choices: Section 35 covers only aerial clearances and doesn't address underground plant at all

Section 35, titled 'Direct-Buried Cable and Cable in Duct Not Part of a Conduit System,' applies to BOTH supply and communication cables in direct-buried or open-duct installations — the distinguishing factor is location type (open earth vs. enclosed structure), not cable type
Section 35 applies only to communication cables; supply cables are covered exclusively under Section 34
Section 35 only applies to cables inside manholes and enclosed conduit systems
pool.explanation: Section 35 covers direct-buried cable and cable in duct not part of an enclosed conduit system, applying to both supply and communication cables — the key distinction driving which section applies is the physical location context (open earth/open duct vs. an enclosed underground structure), not the cable's ownership or utility type.
pool.citation: NESC C2 Section 35, confirmed via multiple independent utility/engineering technical sources.

pool.prompt: A fiber cable is being pulled into an existing manhole on a metro distribution route. Which NESC section governs the separation and installation requirements for this cable inside the manhole?
choices: Section 35, since it covers all underground cable installations universally
Section 32, the general vertical-clearance rule used for aerial spans

Section 34, titled 'Cable in Underground Structures' — this section applies when cables (both supply and communication) are inside enclosed underground structures such as manholes and handholes; Section 35 applies instead to cable in the open earth or open duct
Section 250, the loading-district rule from the T05 aerial-design topic
pool.explanation: Section 34 specifically governs cable inside enclosed underground structures (manholes, handholes) — once the fiber enters the manhole, Section 34's installation requirements apply, distinct from Section 35's open-earth/open-duct scope.
pool.citation: NESC C2 Section 34 ("cable in underground structures," including general requirements, installation, and grounding/bonding subsections).

pool.prompt: A bore crew is installing communication conduit under a road where a direct-buried electric supply cable crosses at a 90-degree angle. What is the recommended field-practice separation at this crossing, beyond the code-minimum figure?
choices: Exactly the code minimum with no additional margin, since exceeding it wastes excavation depth

Field practice commonly targets 12 inches of vertical separation — even though NESC §35/Rule 354 sets a code-minimum figure, the extra margin accounts for typical utility locate tolerance (often plus-or-minus 18 inches), meaning an existing supply cable could be 6-18 inches from its marked location; designing to 12 inches covers both the locate error and the code minimum simultaneously
0 inches — direct crossings are exempt from any separation requirement
10 feet, a figure with no relationship to locate tolerance or code minimums
pool.explanation: The 12-inch field-practice target is deliberately larger than the bare code minimum specifically to absorb locate-tolerance uncertainty — since an existing utility's marked position can be off by more than a foot, designing only to the code-minimum separation risks an actual field separation well below that minimum once real utility positions are confirmed.

pool.prompt: APWA orange warning tape buried above a communication conduit serves what purpose?
choices: It provides electrical grounding continuity for the buried conduit

It is buried 6-12 inches above the conduit (much shallower than the conduit itself) as a visual warning — if an excavator digging in that location hits the tape, they see a 'CAUTION — COMMUNICATION CABLE BELOW' warning before the shovel or bucket reaches the actual conduit; it doesn't provide separation distance or electrical function, only advance warning
It provides the required minimum separation distance from parallel utilities
It marks the exact centerline of the conduit for future 811 locates with GPS-level precision
pool.explanation: Warning tape's function is purely as an advance visual warning, buried intentionally shallower than the conduit it protects — it intercepts excavation before the bucket reaches the actual cable, but provides no separation-distance credit and no electrical/locating function of its own.
pool.citation: APWA Utility Color Code; Common Ground Alliance Best Practices excavation-safety guidance — reused from T06-L06 verification.

pool.prompt: A designer is laying out an underground fiber route that will run parallel to an existing direct-buried electric supply cable for 400 feet in the same residential-street ROW corridor. Which NESC section primarily governs the separation requirement for this parallel run?
choices: Section 34, since any two utilities sharing a corridor are automatically treated as being in an underground structure

Section 35 ('Direct-Buried Cable and Cable in Duct Not Part of a Conduit System') applies here — the fiber conduit is in a bored or open-trench run through open earth, not inside an enclosed underground structure; the specific supply-to-communication parallel-separation requirement lives within Section 35's Rule 354
Section 250, the same loading-district rule that governs aerial ice/wind design
No NESC section applies to parallel (non-crossing) runs; only crossing geometry is regulated
pool.explanation: Because the fiber conduit here is a bored/open-trench installation through open earth (not inside a manhole or enclosed structure), Section 35 — specifically Rule 354's separation requirement — is the applicable governing section, distinct from Section 34's enclosed-structure scope.

pool.prompt: A design shows communication conduit running in the same trench as a residential electric supply at 18 inches cover, with only 4 inches of horizontal separation in the parallel trench. Is this acceptable per NESC §35/Rule 354 and field best practice?
choices: Yes — any horizontal separation greater than zero is compliant regardless of the specific distance

No — NESC §35/Rule 354 requires at minimum roughly 6 inches of horizontal separation for parallel communication-to-supply conduit runs [exact figure per the current NESC C2 edition — the standard is paywalled and values may be updated]; at 4 inches, this design is non-compliant, and field best practice (driven by locate tolerance) calls for 12 inches or more — the fix is to re-route the trench or add a separation board between the conduits
Yes, as long as the electric supply voltage is under 600V
No — any parallel run in the same trench is prohibited under all circumstances regardless of separation distance
pool.explanation: A 4-inch horizontal separation falls short of both the NESC §35/Rule 354 code-minimum figure and the more conservative field-practice target discussed in Q3 — this is a genuine non-compliance that requires either re-routing the trench or adding a physical separation board, not a marginal case.
pool.citation: NESC C2 Section 35 / Rule 354 (exact current numeric separation figure is in the paywalled primary standard — hedged per the T01/T05 precedent for paywalled-standard values).

pool.prompt: Why does the NESC's underground framework distinguish between Section 34 (enclosed structures) and Section 35 (open earth/open duct) rather than using a single unified underground-cable rule?
choices: The distinction is arbitrary and has no functional engineering basis

The physical installation context genuinely differs between the two scenarios — cable inside an enclosed structure (a manhole) has different access, ventilation, and mechanical-protection conditions than cable buried directly in open earth, which justifies separate rule sets tailored to each context's actual physical/safety conditions rather than a one-size-fits-all approach
Section 34 only exists for historical reasons and has been effectively superseded by Section 35 in current practice
The distinction only matters for supply cable, never for communication cable
pool.explanation: The Section 34/35 split reflects a genuine engineering distinction — enclosed-structure and open-earth/open-duct installations present different physical conditions (access, ventilation, mechanical protection) that justify tailored requirements for each context, consistent with the broader NESC pattern (seen in T05's Rules 232/235/250/261) of addressing distinct design dimensions with distinct rules rather than a single blanket requirement.

pool.prompt: A cable route starts as a direct-buried open-trench run (Section 35 scope), then enters a manhole for a splice point, then continues as direct-buried conduit on the other side. Does a single NESC section govern the entire route, or does the governing section change along the route?
choices: A single section governs the entire route from end to end, chosen by whichever section applied at the route's starting point

The governing section changes along the route based on the actual physical installation context at each point — Section 35 applies to the open-trench segments on either side, while Section 34 applies specifically to the portion inside the manhole; a designer needs to apply the correct section to each physical context along the route, not assume one section covers the whole path
Neither section applies once a manhole is involved anywhere on the route
Only Section 34 applies to the entire route, since a manhole is present somewhere along it
pool.explanation: Since Section 34 and Section 35 are distinguished by physical installation context (enclosed structure vs. open earth/duct) rather than by the overall route or project, a single route can legitimately transition between the two governing sections at different points — this is the same segment-specific-requirement pattern seen elsewhere in this training (e.g., T05's per-span grade-of-construction determination), applied here to NESC underground-cable sections.
